title: Why Are My Dog’s Eyes Red? Common Causes and When It’s Urgent
description: Red eyes in dogs can come from irritation, conjunctivitis, dry eye, injury, glaucoma, uveitis, or other eye disease.
summary: Red eyes in dogs can come from irritation, conjunctivitis, dry eye, injury, glaucoma, uveitis, or other eye disease.
primaryKeyword: why are my dog's eyes red
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog with mildly red eye being gently examined in natural light
content:
Red eyes in dogs can come from irritation, conjunctivitis, dry eye, injury, glaucoma, uveitis, or other eye disease.

Quick Answer

Red eyes can follow mild irritation, allergy, dry eye, injury, inflammation inside the eye, or abnormal eye pressure. Because painful eye disease can worsen quickly, sudden redness with squinting, cloudiness, a changed pupil, marked discharge, trauma, or vision loss needs prompt veterinary assessment.

What to Look For

Compare both eyes in the same light. Note redness, squinting, discharge, cloudiness, pupil size, rubbing, trauma, and any apparent vision change. Prevent rubbing and do not use unprescribed eye drops.

Common Causes

1. Minor irritation

Dust, wind, shampoo, or another irritant can redden the surface tissues. Mild irritation should improve after the exposure ends; persistent pain or redness needs a closer look.

2. Conjunctivitis

Inflammation of the conjunctiva can cause redness and discharge, but the underlying trigger may be infectious, allergic, irritant, or secondary to another eye problem.

3. Dry eye

Inadequate tear production can leave the eye red, uncomfortable, and coated with thick discharge. Tear production must be measured to confirm it.

4. Corneal injury

A scratch or ulcer can cause marked pain, squinting, tearing, and redness. Corneal damage can progress quickly and should not be treated with leftover eye medication.

5. Glaucoma or uveitis

Abnormal pressure or inflammation inside the eye can cause redness, pain, cloudiness, pupil changes, and vision loss. These are time-sensitive veterinary problems.

What You Can Do Safely

Compare both eyes in the same light. Note redness, squinting, discharge, cloudiness, pupil size, rubbing, trauma, and any apparent vision change. Prevent rubbing and do not use unprescribed eye drops.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Seek prompt or urgent care for severe eye pain, persistent squinting, cloudiness, a changed pupil, an enlarged-looking eye, trauma, sudden vision loss, or rapidly worsening redness. Eye emergencies can threaten vision even when the dog otherwise seems well.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.

Bottom Line

Red eyes in dogs can come from irritation, conjunctivitis, dry eye, injury, glaucoma, uveitis, or other eye disease. The pattern and accompanying signs matter more than appearance alone, and persistent or worsening problems deserve professional assessment.

title: Why Does My Dog Have Eye Discharge? Clear, Yellow and Green Discharge Explained
description: Dog eye discharge may be harmless tear debris or a sign of irritation, infection, dry eye, injury, eyelid problems, or other disease.

content:
Dog eye discharge may be harmless tear debris or a sign of irritation, infection, dry eye, injury, eyelid problems, or other disease.

Quick Answer

A small amount of clear or dried tear debris can be normal, but persistent yellow, green, bloody, or increasing discharge can accompany irritation, infection, dry eye, eyelid problems, or corneal injury. Squinting, cloudiness, pain, or vision change makes the problem more urgent.

What to Look For

Note the color, amount, consistency, and whether one or both eyes are affected. Gently wipe external debris with clean damp gauze if the eye is comfortable, but do not flush or medicate a painful eye without veterinary guidance.

Common Causes

1. Normal tear debris

A small amount of clear moisture or dried debris near the inner corner can occur in otherwise comfortable eyes.

2. Irritation or conjunctival inflammation

Dust, hair, allergens, or inflammation can increase tearing or mucus. Ongoing redness or discomfort suggests more than routine debris.

3. Dry eye

Reduced tear production often causes thick, sticky discharge and chronic irritation. Diagnosis requires veterinary testing.

4. Corneal injury or foreign material

A scratch or material trapped around the eye can produce sudden tearing, discharge, rubbing, and squinting.

5. Eyelid or tear-drainage problems

Abnormal eyelid position, lashes, or tear drainage can cause recurrent discharge and staining and may require an eye examination.

What You Can Do Safely

Note the color, amount, consistency, and whether one or both eyes are affected. Gently wipe external debris with clean damp gauze if the eye is comfortable, but do not flush or medicate a painful eye without veterinary guidance.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Contact a veterinarian for persistent colored discharge, recurrent discharge, redness, rubbing, or eyelid abnormalities. Sudden pain, marked squinting, cloudiness, trauma, pupil changes, or vision loss needs prompt assessment.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.

title: Why Do My Dog’s Ears Smell Bad? Ear Infection, Yeast and Allergy Clues
description: A strong ear odor can accompany yeast or bacterial overgrowth, inflammation, moisture, allergies, parasites, or foreign material.
summary: A strong ear odor can accompany yeast or bacterial overgrowth, inflammation, moisture, allergies, parasites, or foreign material.

author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog calmly having the outer ear checked by its owner
content:
A strong ear odor can accompany yeast or bacterial overgrowth, inflammation, moisture, allergies, parasites, or foreign material.

Quick Answer

Strong ear odor is not a diagnosis. Yeast or bacterial overgrowth, inflammation, moisture, allergy, parasites, or foreign material can contribute. Odor with pain, redness, discharge, swelling, or repeated head shaking should be examined rather than treated blindly at home.

What to Look For

Look only at the visible outer ear and entrance to the canal. Record odor, redness, discharge, swelling, scratching, and head shaking. Keep the ear dry and avoid inserting swabs or pouring products into a painful ear.

Common Causes

1. Yeast or bacterial overgrowth

Microbes normally live on skin, but inflamed ear canals can support overgrowth that produces strong odor, discharge, and discomfort.

2. Moisture

Swimming or bathing can leave a susceptible ear canal damp, but moisture alone does not explain persistent pain or discharge.

3. Allergic skin disease

Allergies commonly affect the ears and can create recurrent inflammation that predisposes them to secondary infection.

4. Ear mites

Mites are more common in some populations and can cause intense itching and dark debris; an examination helps distinguish them from other causes.

5. Foreign material

Plant material or debris can trigger sudden one-sided head shaking, scratching, pain, and secondary inflammation.

What You Can Do Safely

Look only at the visible outer ear and entrance to the canal. Record odor, redness, discharge, swelling, scratching, and head shaking. Keep the ear dry and avoid inserting swabs or pouring products into a painful ear.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Arrange veterinary care for strong persistent odor, pain, discharge, marked redness, swelling, or recurrent ear disease. Head tilt, loss of balance, severe pain, or neurologic signs increase urgency.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.

title: Why Does My Dog Keep Scratching His Ears? Common Causes and What to Check

author: Virixoo Editorial Team

content:
Frequent ear scratching can signal infection, allergy, parasites, moisture, foreign material, or irritation.

Quick Answer

Frequent ear scratching usually means the ear or nearby skin is itchy or uncomfortable. Infection, allergy, mites, moisture, or foreign material are possibilities. Persistent scratching, pain, odor, discharge, swelling, or head tilt warrants veterinary assessment.

What to Look For

Check the outer ear for redness, discharge, odor, swelling, and scratches without probing the canal. Prevent excessive self-trauma if possible and keep the ear dry until the cause is known.

Common Causes

1. Ear infection or inflammation

An inflamed ear canal is itchy and painful, and may have odor, redness, or discharge. Cytology or other testing helps guide treatment.

2. Allergy

Environmental or food-related allergy can produce recurrent ear itching, often along with paw licking or other skin signs.

3. Ear mites

Mites can cause intense itching and dark debris, particularly in younger dogs or those exposed to affected animals.

4. Foreign material

Grass awns and other debris can cause abrupt, vigorous scratching or head shaking, often affecting one ear.

5. Moisture or local irritation

Water, grooming products, or mechanical irritation can aggravate a sensitive ear, but persistent signs should not be assumed to be simple irritation.

What You Can Do Safely

Check the outer ear for redness, discharge, odor, swelling, and scratches without probing the canal. Prevent excessive self-trauma if possible and keep the ear dry until the cause is known.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Seek veterinary assessment for persistent scratching, pain, odor, discharge, swelling, or repeated episodes. A head tilt, balance disturbance, severe pain, or sudden one-sided signs after outdoor exposure deserve faster attention.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

title: Why Does My Dog Have a Skin Rash? Common Causes and Warning Signs
description: Dog rashes can be caused by allergies, parasites, infections, contact irritation, insect bites, moisture, or underlying disease.

content:
Dog rashes can be caused by allergies, parasites, infections, contact irritation, insect bites, moisture, or underlying disease.

Quick Answer

A skin rash can have many causes, including contact irritation, allergy, parasites, infection, moisture, or trauma. Distribution, itch, pain, odor, discharge, and speed of spread are more useful than appearance alone; rapidly worsening or painful lesions need veterinary attention.

What to Look For

Photograph the rash, note where it began and whether it is spreading, and check for itch, pain, odor, moisture, pustules, crusts, parasites, or a recent product or environmental exposure.

Common Causes

1. Contact irritation

Plants, cleaners, grooming products, or other substances can irritate exposed skin, especially where contact was concentrated.

2. Allergy

Allergic skin disease often causes itch and recurrent inflammation on the paws, face, ears, belly, or other characteristic areas.

3. Parasites

Fleas, mites, and other parasites can produce itching, bumps, crusts, or hair loss; distribution and parasite prevention history are useful clues.

4. Bacterial or yeast infection

Secondary infection can add odor, pustules, crusts, greasiness, pain, or discharge to already inflamed skin.

5. Moisture, friction, or trauma

Skin folds, wet coats, rubbing equipment, and self-trauma can damage the skin barrier and create localized rash-like lesions.

What You Can Do Safely

Photograph the rash, note where it began and whether it is spreading, and check for itch, pain, odor, moisture, pustules, crusts, parasites, or a recent product or environmental exposure.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Contact a veterinarian when a rash is spreading, painful, recurrent, infected-looking, or accompanied by feverish behavior, lethargy, facial swelling, or significant illness. Breathing difficulty or rapidly developing facial swelling is an emergency.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.

title: Why Does My Dog Have Dandruff? Dry Skin, Allergies and Other Causes
description: White flakes in a dog's coat can reflect dry skin, seborrhea, allergies, parasites, infection, grooming issues, or underlying disease.
summary: White flakes in a dog's coat can reflect dry skin, seborrhea, allergies, parasites, infection, grooming issues, or underlying disease.

author: Virixoo Editorial Team

content:
White flakes in a dog's coat can reflect dry skin, seborrhea, allergies, parasites, infection, grooming issues, or underlying disease.

Quick Answer

Allergies can affect a dog's skin, paws, ears, and sometimes digestive tract, but itching alone cannot identify the trigger. Recurrent ear disease, paw licking, seasonal itching, or widespread skin inflammation deserves a veterinary plan rather than repeated trial-and-error remedies.

What to Look For

Map where the dog itches and track season, diet, parasite prevention, ear problems, paw licking, and skin infections. Avoid repeatedly changing foods or applying multiple products at once because that can make the pattern harder to interpret.

Common Causes

1. Environmental allergy

Pollens, molds, dust mites, and other environmental allergens can contribute to recurrent itch affecting paws, ears, face, or skin.

2. Food allergy

Food allergy is possible but cannot be diagnosed from symptoms alone; a properly designed elimination diet may be needed when a veterinarian considers it appropriate.

3. Flea allergy

A flea-allergic dog can itch intensely after very limited flea exposure, often around the rump and tail base.

4. Secondary skin or ear infection

Allergic inflammation can make bacterial or yeast overgrowth more likely, adding odor, discharge, redness, or worsening itch.

5. Other itchy skin disease

Parasites and non-allergic skin conditions can mimic allergy, so ruling out competing causes is an important part of diagnosis.

What You Can Do Safely

Map where the dog itches and track season, diet, parasite prevention, ear problems, paw licking, and skin infections. Avoid repeatedly changing foods or applying multiple products at once because that can make the pattern harder to interpret.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Veterinary assessment is appropriate for recurrent or significant itching, repeated ear infections, raw skin, hair loss, or suspected food allergy. Sudden facial swelling, breathing difficulty, collapse, or rapidly worsening hives requires emergency care.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.

title: Does My Dog Have Allergies? Signs, Common Triggers and What to Do
description: Dogs with allergies often develop itchy skin, paw licking, recurring ear trouble, inflamed skin, or sometimes digestive signs.

author: Virixoo Editorial Team

content:
Dogs with allergies often develop itchy skin, paw licking, recurring ear trouble, inflamed skin, or sometimes digestive signs.

Quick Answer

A hot spot is a rapidly inflamed, moist, painful skin lesion often worsened by licking or scratching. Keep the dog from traumatizing the area and arrange veterinary care when the lesion is painful, spreading, oozing, foul-smelling, or difficult to keep dry.

What to Look For

Prevent licking or scratching as safely as possible and keep the area clean and dry. Do not scrub aggressively, clip a painful dog without appropriate restraint, or apply irritating home remedies.

Common Causes

1. Self-trauma from itching

Licking, chewing, and scratching can rapidly damage skin and create a moist, inflamed lesion.

2. Allergy or insect bites

An itchy trigger such as allergy, fleas, or another bite can start the cycle of self-trauma.

3. Moisture trapped in the coat

Wet or dense coats can retain moisture against the skin and make local inflammation harder to dry.

4. Ear or nearby pain

Dogs may scratch skin near a painful ear or other local problem, so the apparent skin lesion may not be the original trigger.

5. Secondary infection

Damaged moist skin can develop bacterial overgrowth, increasing pain, odor, discharge, and lesion size.

What You Can Do Safely

Prevent licking or scratching as safely as possible and keep the area clean and dry. Do not scrub aggressively, clip a painful dog without appropriate restraint, or apply irritating home remedies.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Hot spots that are rapidly enlarging, very painful, foul-smelling, oozing, or difficult to protect should be examined promptly. Lethargy, feverish behavior, extensive skin involvement, or severe pain raises urgency.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.

title: How to Tell if Your Dog Has Fleas: Signs, Flea Dirt and What to Check
description: Learn how to look for fleas and flea dirt, where fleas often hide, and why persistent itching may need veterinary treatment.
summary: Learn how to look for fleas and flea dirt, where fleas often hide, and why persistent itching may need veterinary treatment.
primaryKeyword: how to tell if your dog has fleas
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Owner using a flea comb on a dog's coat over a light towel
content:
Learn how to look for fleas and flea dirt, where fleas often hide, and why persistent itching may need veterinary treatment.

Quick Answer

Fleas can be hard to see, so check for both live insects and flea dirt, especially around the rump, tail base, abdomen, and groin. Persistent itching can continue even when few fleas are visible, particularly in dogs with flea allergy.

What to Look For

Use a flea comb over several body areas and inspect bedding. If parasite treatment is needed, use a product appropriate for the dog's species, age, weight, and health status and follow veterinary or label guidance exactly.

Common Causes

1. Live fleas

Adult fleas move quickly through the coat and may be easiest to find around the rump, tail base, abdomen, or groin.

2. Flea dirt

Dark specks of flea feces can be easier to find than the fleas themselves; when moistened on a white surface, digested blood may create a reddish-brown halo.

3. Flea allergy dermatitis

Sensitive dogs may develop intense itching and skin lesions from relatively few flea bites.

4. Environmental infestation

Most flea life stages are not on the dog, so recurrent exposure from the environment can continue even after adult fleas are removed.

5. Another cause of itching

Failure to find fleas does not prove that itching is unrelated to parasites, nor does it exclude allergy, infection, or other skin disease.

What You Can Do Safely

Use a flea comb over several body areas and inspect bedding. If parasite treatment is needed, use a product appropriate for the dog's species, age, weight, and health status and follow veterinary or label guidance exactly.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Seek veterinary advice for persistent intense itching, infected skin, anemia-like weakness or pale gums, very young or medically fragile dogs, or failure of an appropriate flea-control plan. Never use a dog-only flea product on a cat sharing the home unless it is specifically labeled safe for cats.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.

title: Why Does My Dog Have a Lump Under the Skin? When to Get It Checked
description: Lumps in dogs can be benign or serious, and appearance alone cannot reliably identify them. Learn what to record and why sampling is often needed.
summary: Lumps in dogs can be benign or serious, and appearance alone cannot reliably identify them. Learn what to record and why sampling is often needed.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Owner gently noticing a small lump beneath a dog's coat
content:
Lumps in dogs can be benign or serious, and appearance alone cannot reliably identify them. Learn what to record and why sampling is often needed.

Quick Answer

A lump under the skin cannot be reliably identified by touch or appearance alone. Record its location and size and arrange examination for a new or changing mass; sampling with a needle or other testing is often needed to determine what it is.

What to Look For

Measure the lump in two dimensions, photograph it with a ruler for scale, and note location, texture, mobility, pain, skin changes, and growth. Do not squeeze, lance, or repeatedly manipulate it.

Common Causes

1. Lipoma

Fatty masses are common in adult dogs and are often soft and movable, but feel alone cannot confirm that a lump is a lipoma.

2. Cyst or other benign skin mass

Some cysts and benign growths remain small and stable, while others become inflamed or rupture. Identification still requires veterinary assessment.

3. Abscess or inflammatory swelling

Pain, warmth, redness, rapid enlargement, or discharge can suggest inflammation or infection rather than a stable benign mass.

4. Enlarged lymph node

A lump in a lymph-node location may reflect local or systemic disease and should be interpreted with the dog's overall examination.

5. Tumor

Some tumors are harmless and others are serious; size, firmness, and appearance cannot reliably separate them, which is why sampling is valuable.

What You Can Do Safely

Measure the lump in two dimensions, photograph it with a ruler for scale, and note location, texture, mobility, pain, skin changes, and growth. Do not squeeze, lance, or repeatedly manipulate it.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Every new or changing lump deserves veterinary assessment rather than visual diagnosis. Faster evaluation is appropriate for rapid growth, pain, ulceration, bleeding, fixation to deeper tissue, or illness elsewhere in the body.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.

title: Why Is My Dog Breathing Fast While Resting? What to Count and When to Worry
description: Fast breathing at rest can occur with heat, stress or recent activity, but persistent rapid breathing may also reflect pain, fever, heart or lung disease, anemia, or other illness.

content:
Fast breathing at rest can occur with heat, stress or recent activity, but persistent rapid breathing may also reflect pain, fever, heart or lung disease, anemia, or other illness.

Quick Answer

Hair loss can result from scratching, parasites, infection, allergy, hormonal disease, friction, or other skin problems. The pattern—itchy versus non-itchy, focal versus widespread, inflamed versus normal-looking skin—helps guide the veterinary workup.

What to Look For

Photograph the distribution of hair loss and inspect the skin for redness, scale, crusts, sores, parasites, and broken hairs. Track itch, grooming, medications, diet, weight, thirst, and whether the pattern is spreading.

Common Causes

1. Self-trauma from itching

Repeated scratching, licking, or chewing can break hairs or remove them completely, often leaving inflamed skin.

2. Parasites

Fleas and mites can produce patchy hair loss, itching, crusting, or scaling. Parasite prevention history helps but does not replace examination.

3. Skin infection

Bacterial or fungal disease can cause focal or spreading alopecia with redness, scale, crusts, or odor.

4. Allergic skin disease

Chronic allergy can cause recurrent itch, paw licking, ear disease, and secondary hair loss.

5. Hormonal or systemic disease

Some endocrine and systemic disorders produce more symmetrical, less itchy hair loss and other changes such as weight, thirst, skin texture, or energy.

What You Can Do Safely

Photograph the distribution of hair loss and inspect the skin for redness, scale, crusts, sores, parasites, and broken hairs. Track itch, grooming, medications, diet, weight, thirst, and whether the pattern is spreading.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Arrange veterinary care for unexplained, spreading, recurrent, or non-regrowing hair loss, especially with itch, sores, infection, weight change, increased thirst, lethargy, or other systemic signs.

What to Tell Your Veterinarian

Share when the problem began, how it has changed, whether it affects one area or several, and any photos that document progression. Include recent medications, parasite prevention, grooming, diet changes, swimming, travel, outdoor exposure, and other new symptoms.
